title: The Growing Problem With Personal Finance YouTuber "Influencers"
summary: Critique of personal finance YouTubers: predictions, invented rules, and survivorship-biased success stories that imply dropping out and leveraging up works for everyone.

assertions.quote: Financial predictions are almost impossible to make

verdicts.note: Success rates decline with days traded exactly as in casino roulette, and the authors treat day trading as gambling-like; predictability of prices itself is not tested.

Authors conclude that for prospective day traders trading to learn is no more rational or profitable than playing roulette, yet under 3% of traders are predictably profitable, so it is not pure chance.

assertions.quote: even the largest financial firms in the world filled with teams of PHD Quantitative Analysts struggle to outperform regular market returns consistently
The generally accepted rate of return for a well-diversified portfolio is anywhere between 6% all the way up to 12%
Nobody is making a video about how they lost their life savings trying to flip homes.
take out a 10:1 leveraged position on a house, and you are an investment genius. Most people don’t realise how risky real estate can be.

verdicts.note: In leveraged CFDs ESMA finds leverage increases possible losses as it increases possible profit, and for retail investors raises the probability of a larger loss more; the claim's debt-timing context is not covered.

FCA price analysis: at 500:1 leverage with a 50% close-out, retail clients are closed out on the losing side 81% of the time and lose all or more than their margin 44% of the time; leverage magnifies losses (more than gains for retail CFD clients), but the claim's debt-timing context is not covered.

assertions.quote: everything you need to know about personal finance should be able to fit on a postcard
if they did they sure wouldn’t be sharing them on a YouTube video
which has worked for them, but will not work for most people

verdicts.note: Earnings data show degree holders earn more on average; outliers exist.

Earnings gains from becoming an entrepreneur are confined to high-skill rule-breakers: high-wage, high-illicit individuals gain 27% when they incorporate while low-wage, low-illicit individuals lose about 6%, and those who incorporate were already successful, well-educated salaried workers from higher-income families; the paper says nothing about dropping out, and its entrepreneurs are the best-educated group.
